name: Labor Productivity
description: Labor productivity measures economic output relative to the labor used to produce it. Understanding Iran's productivity requires distinguishing output per worker from output per hour, and separating changes in production from changes in employment.

seo.title: Labor Productivity in Iran: Measures and Interpretation
seo.description: Understand output per worker, output per hour, purchasing power comparisons, and the evidence needed to assess Iran's labor productivity.

content.heading: What productivity measures
content.content:
Labor productivity relates the value of production to the labor used in producing it. Two common measures divide gross domestic product, or GDP, by the number of employed people or by total hours worked. GDP measures production across the economy; it is not a measure of the wages workers receive. The International Labour Organization, a United Nations agency specializing in work and employment, identifies both workers and hours as possible denominators. [s1]

The distinction matters when reading evidence about Iran. Output per worker can change because production changes, because employment changes, or because both move together. Output per hour additionally accounts for changes in working time. A comparison between the two therefore needs consistent definitions of employment and hours, rather than an assumption that every employed person works an identical schedule. [s1][s2]

content.heading: An indicator of the production system
content.content:
A productivity statistic should not be read as a score for individual effort. Machinery, technology, intermediate inputs, organization, and economies of scale all affect the output associated with an hour of work. The OECD, an international economic research organization, explicitly cautions that labor productivity only partly reflects workers' personal capacities or effort. [s2]

This also explains why a rise in aggregate productivity needs interpretation. It can reflect investment and innovation, but it can also accompany a reduction in the employment of workers in activities with lower measured output per worker. A higher average does not, by itself, demonstrate that employment opportunities improved. Productivity and the extent to which an economy uses available labor are related but distinct dimensions of economic performance. [s2]

Multifactor productivity asks a different question: how much output is produced relative to a combination of inputs, commonly labor and capital. Labor productivity can rise when workers have more equipment available, even without an improvement in the efficiency of the combined inputs. These measures should therefore retain their separate names and definitions. [s3]

content.heading: Reading the available Iran series
content.content:
The World Bank publishes an Iran indicator titled GDP per person employed, measured in constant 2021 purchasing-power-parity dollars. Purchasing power parity, usually abbreviated PPP, provides a basis for comparing purchasing power across economies. The indicator's constant-price basis distinguishes it from a current-dollar measure whose movements can reflect changing prices and currency conversion. Its metadata identifies the figures as staff estimates using employment, population, GDP, and PPP inputs from several international organizations. [s4]

The ILO also lists output per worker and output per hour in constant 2021 international dollars, alongside a separate constant 2015 US-dollar series. These are distinct statistical products; their price bases and units must remain visible. The ILO explains that its modelled database combines nationally reported information with estimates where information is missing. [s5]

The inspected pages established the available measures but did not expose a verified annual Iran table suitable for reproduction here. This page consequently makes no claim about the direction or size of Iran's recent productivity trend. A completed assessment needs the observations, release vintage, employment coverage, and any revisions before it can connect movements in the indicator to developments in the Iranian economy. [s4][s5]

name: Income Distribution
description: Distribution statistics describe how economic resources differ across people and households. Iran's internationally reported Gini series is based on household expenditure, making it essential to distinguish this measure from the distribution of earnings, income, or wealth.

seo.title: Income Distribution in Iran: Inequality and Household Expenditure
seo.description: Explore Iran's expenditure-based Gini series, its annual movements, and the limits of using household surveys to describe income inequality.

content.heading: What is being distributed?
content.content:
Income distribution concerns how resources are shared across households and individuals, rather than simply how much an economy produces. But the name of a topic does not settle the statistical measure used to study it. The World Bank's Gini indicator can describe either income or consumption expenditure, depending on the underlying survey. These concepts must remain explicit when comparing countries or years. [s3]

The Gini index summarizes inequality on a scale from zero, representing perfect equality, to 100, representing perfect inequality. It is based on the distance between the observed distribution and a hypothetical equal distribution. It does not identify which particular households gained or lost resources, and a single national value cannot describe every difference within a country. [s3]

content.heading: Iran's expenditure-based evidence
content.content:
The Statistical Center of Iran conducts the Household Expenditure and Income Survey, known as HEIS. Despite collecting income information, the survey has a strong expenditure focus. The World Bank describes it as nationally representative, with sampling stratified across urban and rural areas within provinces. Its international poverty and inequality welfare aggregate uses household expenditure per person, adjusted for differences in prices over time and across places. [s2]

This makes the resulting Gini an expenditure-inequality measure. It should not be relabeled as wage inequality, a wealth-concentration measure, or a direct estimate of the share of income received by the richest households. Survey responses are self-reported. Recall periods also differ across items: many expenditures use the previous month, while some less frequent expenditures and income components use the previous year. Estimated values are included for some items that were not purchased. These details matter when interpreting what household resources mean in the published statistics. [s2]

content.heading: An uneven annual pattern
content.content:
The World Bank series reproduced by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis shows an increase from 34.4 in 2012 to 37.4 in 2018, followed by a decline to 34.8 in 2022. The value then rose to 35.9 in 2023. This is an uneven sequence, rather than evidence of a continuous improvement or deterioration. The accompanying dataset preserves the published one-decimal precision. [s1]

These movements describe relative dispersion. They do not establish whether purchasing power increased, whether poverty declined, or which policies caused the changes. Those questions require additional evidence on real household expenditure, prices, and the distribution of gains. Keeping inequality separate from poverty avoids treating a lower Gini as automatic proof that households became better off. The Gini summarizes relative distribution; poverty statistics assess resources against a specified threshold. [s2][s3]

name: Oil & Gas
description: Iran's oil and gas sector connects export earnings with domestic electricity, heating, industry, and petrochemicals. Its large resource base coexists with investment constraints, seasonal supply pressures, and exposure to sanctions and infrastructure disruption.

seo.title: Oil and Gas in Iran: Production, Domestic Demand and Constraints
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to Iran's petroleum and natural gas systems, investment challenges, domestic demand, and dated disruption reports.

content.heading: Two connected energy systems
content.content:
Iran's hydrocarbon economy has two closely connected roles: supplying energy within the country and earning revenue abroad. Oil and natural gas should nevertheless be followed separately. Crude oil, condensate, and other petroleum liquids are not interchangeable statistical categories, while natural gas production must be distinguished from the volumes available after domestic use. The US Energy Information Administration, or EIA, documents the importance of both export markets and domestic consumption in its country analysis. [s1]

Large reserves do not establish how much energy can be delivered at a particular moment. The EIA identifies underinvestment and international sanctions as constraints on Iran's petroleum sector. Its analysis also connects gas availability with electricity generation, industrial activity, and seasonal demand. Reading the sector therefore requires attention to processing, transport, storage, and customers alongside the resources underground. [s1]

content.heading: Oil production and investment
content.content:
The International Energy Agency, or IEA, described a production system with limited spare capacity in its Oil 2025 report. Its account emphasized efforts by domestic firms to counter declining output from existing fields, including the development of equipment and technologies used to support recovery. Maintaining production is consequently a continuing investment task, rather than a one-time consequence of discovering a field. [s2]

The report also discussed expansion opportunities in the West Karun area and contracts intended to raise production. These descriptions establish the existence of development efforts and stated objectives; they do not demonstrate that the resulting capacity was completed. For a reader comparing project announcements, the useful distinctions are between a signed contract, installed facilities, tested capacity, and sustained output. The report's forward-looking assessments should retain their 2025 context. [s2]

This matters when interpreting export figures as well. The IEA reported that changes in Chinese purchasing affected Iranian shipments during 2025. A production opportunity and a dependable market are separate questions: commercial conditions can change even where a field continues operating. The report provides a dated assessment, rather than proof of export conditions at the October 2026 cutoff. [s2]

content.heading: Natural gas and domestic dependence
content.content:
South Pars, the offshore field shared with Qatar, is central to Iran's gas system. On the Qatari side it is known as the North Field. The IEA's second-quarter 2026 gas report identifies South Pars as the cornerstone of Iran's gas-based economy and describes power generation, industry, and household and commercial users as major destinations for domestic supply. [s3]

The field's geography connects offshore production to processing facilities around Assaluyeh on Iran's Persian Gulf coast. Gas processing is an essential link between extraction and usable supply. The same IEA report describes Iran's pipeline exports to Iraq and Türkiye, showing that domestic infrastructure also has consequences for neighboring energy systems. [s3]

content.title: Selected links in Iran's gas system
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["South Pars offshore field"] -->|"Gas for treatment"| B["Assaluyeh processing facilities"]
  B -->|"Processed supply enters"| C["Iranian gas system"]
  C -->|"Domestic supply"| D["Power generation"]
  C -->|"Domestic supply"| E["Industry"]
  C -->|"Domestic supply"| F["Households and businesses"]
  C -->|"Pipeline exports"| G["Iraq and Türkiye"]
```
content.summary: The arrows describe selected physical supply relationships, not ownership or legal authority. The diagram omits other Iranian fields and processing facilities and does not establish uninterrupted flows.

content.heading: Disruption and the limits of a dated snapshot
content.content:
The IEA's second-quarter 2026 report documented attacks affecting gas processing infrastructure in March and April. It explicitly described information about the effects on Iran's gas market as limited. Some assessments of damage and production effects were preliminary or based on local reporting, so they should not be treated as final engineering audits. [s3]

The earlier EIA analysis provides a different kind of baseline: it explains seasonal pressure, limited storage, and the relationship between gas shortages and alternative fuels in power plants. Those structural relationships help explain why energy abundance can coexist with delivery constraints, but a 2024 assessment cannot verify the operating condition of facilities after subsequent disruption. [s1]

A complete cutoff-date account requires verified information on repairs, actual production, export flows, and facility availability. Until that evidence is assembled, the defensible conclusion is that Iran's resource base, infrastructure capacity, and delivered energy supply must be evaluated separately. This page retains the distinction and leaves current operating conditions open for further research.
